subject: Economics
name: Economics, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Economic decision-making and living standards
syllabus: VCE Economics Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

points.title: Microeconomics and macroeconomics
points.brief: Microeconomics studies single markets, consumers and businesses. Macroeconomics studies the whole economy, such as growth, jobs and prices.

points.title: Positive and normative statements
points.brief: A positive statement can be tested against facts. A normative statement gives an opinion about what should happen.

points.title: Factors of production
points.brief: The resources used to make goods and services, natural resources, labour, capital and enterprise.

points.title: The basic economic problem
points.brief: Wants are unlimited but resources are scarce, so every society must decide what and how much to make, how to make it and who gets it.

points.title: Opportunity cost
points.brief: The value of the next best choice given up. Weighing it is the heart of trade-offs and cost-benefit analysis.

points.title: The production possibility frontier
points.brief: A curve showing the most two goods an economy can make with its resources. Points on it are efficient, points inside waste resources, and moving along it shows opportunity cost.

points.title: Economic systems
points.brief: Market, planned, mixed and traditional economies answer the three economic questions in different ways, through prices, the state, both, or custom.

points.title: The three-sector circular flow
points.brief: Households, businesses and government trade resources, income, goods, taxes and services in a loop that shows how money moves through the economy.

points.title: Economic agents and sectors
points.brief: Consumers, businesses and government make the economy's decisions. The private sector is owned by people and firms; the public sector by government.

points.title: The traditional view of consumers
points.brief: Traditional economics assumes consumers act in their own interest, are rational and well informed, and try to get the most satisfaction (utility) from what they buy.

points.title: Marginal thinking
points.brief: A rational decision weighs the extra benefit of one more unit against its extra cost, and stops where they meet.

points.title: Incentives and disincentives
points.brief: Taxes, rebates, subsidies and regulations change what people and businesses choose, by making some actions cheaper and others dearer.

points.title: The traditional view of business and government
points.brief: Traditional economics assumes businesses aim to maximise profit and government aims to maximise living standards, by stabilising the economy, improving efficiency and redistributing income.

points.title: The law of demand
points.brief: As a price rises, the quantity demanded falls, other things equal. A change in price is a movement along the demand curve.

points.title: Factors that shift demand
points.brief: Disposable income, the prices of substitutes and complements, tastes, interest rates, population and consumer confidence shift the whole demand curve.

points.title: The law of supply
points.brief: As a price rises, the quantity supplied rises, because selling more becomes more profitable. A change in price is a movement along the supply curve.

points.title: Factors that shift supply
points.brief: Costs of production, technology, productivity, the weather and other disruptions shift the whole supply curve.

points.title: Market equilibrium
points.brief: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A shortage pushes the price up and a surplus pushes it down.

points.title: Changes in equilibrium
points.brief: A shift in demand or supply moves the market to a new equilibrium price and quantity. Working out the direction of each is the core market skill.

points.title: What a market is
points.brief: Any place or system where buyers and sellers trade, face to face or online. Markets set prices that guide what is made.

points.title: Perfect competition
points.brief: A perfectly competitive market has many small buyers and sellers, identical products, full information and free entry, so no one controls the price.

points.title: Relative prices and resource allocation
points.brief: When one good's price rises relative to others, producers move resources toward it and consumers move away from it.

points.title: Market structures
points.brief: Markets range from perfect competition through monopolistic competition and oligopoly to monopoly. More market power usually means higher prices and less efficient use of resources.

points.title: Business strategies to raise profit
points.brief: Firms may charge different groups different prices, sell several brands of one product, or act against competition in ways the Competition and Consumer Act bans.

points.title: Traditional and behavioural economics
points.brief: Traditional economics assumes rational, informed, self-interested people. Behavioural economics tests this with experiments and finds people often act otherwise.

points.title: Bounded rationality
points.brief: People have limited time, information and brain power, so they settle for decisions that are good enough rather than the best.

points.title: Bounded willpower
points.brief: People often choose what feels good now over what serves them later, such as spending instead of saving.

points.title: Bounded self-interest
points.brief: People care about fairness and others, not only themselves, so they donate, tip and refuse unfair offers.

points.title: How government uses behavioural insights
points.brief: Governments steer choices with defaults, reminders and how options are presented, such as opt-out superannuation or organ donor sign-up, without banning anything.

points.title: How businesses use behavioural insights
points.brief: Businesses use framing, anchoring, loss aversion, free trials that roll over and limited-time offers to influence what consumers buy.

units.title: Unit 2: Economic issues and living standards

points.title: The purpose of economic activity
points.brief: Economic activity is the making, selling and buying of goods and services. Its purpose is to meet needs and wants and so raise living standards.

points.title: Material living standards
points.brief: Access to goods and services, often measured by real GDP per person.

points.title: Non-material living standards
points.brief: Things money cannot buy directly, such as health, safety, freedom, the environment and leisure time.

points.title: The five-sector circular flow
points.brief: Adds financial institutions and the overseas sector to households, businesses and government, with saving, tax and imports leaking out and investment, spending and exports flowing in.

points.title: Measuring economic growth
points.brief: GDP is the market value of final goods and services made in a year. Growth is measured by the change in real GDP, which removes price rises.

points.title: Limits of GDP
points.brief: Real GDP per person misses unpaid work, the environment, how income is shared and leisure, so it is an incomplete measure of living standards.

points.title: Measures beyond GDP
points.brief: Measures such as the Human Development Index combine income with health and education to give a fuller picture of living standards.

points.title: The business cycle
points.brief: The economy moves through phases of expansion, peak, contraction and trough, rather than growing at a steady rate.

points.title: Economic indicators
points.brief: Leading indicators change before the economy does, such as building approvals; coincident ones move with it, such as GDP; lagging ones change after, such as unemployment.

points.title: Aggregate demand
points.brief: Total spending: consumption, investment, government spending, and exports less imports. Confidence, interest rates and income change it.

points.title: Aggregate supply
points.brief: The total output businesses can make, set by the quantity and quality of resources, costs of production, technology and productivity.

points.title: Benefits of economic growth
points.brief: Growth can raise incomes, create jobs, fund better health and education and help a country develop.

points.title: Costs of economic growth
points.brief: Growth can bring boom and bust, congestion, pollution, environmental damage, wider inequality and affluenza, the stress of always wanting more.

chapters.title: Issue: the distribution of income and wealth

points.title: Income and wealth inequality
points.brief: Income is a flow of money earned; wealth is a stock of assets owned. Both are spread unevenly, and wealth more so.

points.title: Measuring inequality
points.brief: The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient show how evenly income or wealth is shared. A Gini of 0 is perfectly equal.

points.title: Causes and effects of inequality
points.brief: Differences in skills, jobs, inheritance and age drive inequality. Too much can harm social cohesion and growth.

points.title: Views on inequality
points.brief: Households, workers, businesses and governments see inequality differently, weighing fairness, incentives to work and the cost of support.

points.title: Reducing inequality
points.brief: Progressive taxes, welfare payments, minimum wages and public education and health reduce inequality.

points.title: What environmental sustainability means
points.brief: Meeting needs now without leaving later generations worse off, tracked with measures such as emissions per person and land and water use.

points.title: Climate change as an economic issue
points.brief: Emissions impose costs on others not paid by the polluter, a negative externality, which markets alone do not fix.

points.title: Views on sustainability
points.brief: Households, businesses, governments and groups such as farmers or miners weigh the costs and benefits of acting on the environment differently.

points.title: Policies on emissions
points.brief: Local, national and international responses, such as carbon pricing, clean energy subsidies, regulation and global agreements, each try to cut emissions at least cost.

points.title: Trade-offs between goals
points.brief: Pursuing one aim, such as faster growth, can cost another, such as the environment or equity, so policy involves choices.
